title: When the Line Breaks Down
blurb: Deal with problems on the phone

steps.html:
Four phone calls, each one going wrong in a different way — a cold caller, a friend who will not hang up, two children and a garage bill, and a line that keeps dropping. Then a film about languages that almost disappeared.

  • Handle problems on the phone with the right phrase
  • Use the present perfect to give news
  • Follow a documentary and take notes from it
  • Write an informal email giving news

steps.title: Which reply ends a sales call most politely but most firmly?
options: I'm a bit busy, could you call back later?
I don't take sales calls. Would you remove my details from your database, please?

steps.answer: I'd better get off the phone — I've got a meeting in five minutes.

steps.title: Read between the lines.
steps.sub: Mrs Carter does not simply say no. She asks the caller to remove her details from the database.
steps.prompt: Why does she do that?
options: Because she is not allowed to end the call herself.
Because refusing once stops this call, and removing the details stops the next one.
Because she wants to know what the company holds about her.
steps.answer: Because refusing once stops this call, and removing the details stops the next one.
steps.why: It is the difference between handling an interruption and preventing it. Her request is about every future call, not this one.

steps.title: Language noticing.
steps.sub: Compare 'I'd better get off the phone — I've got a meeting' with 'Stop talking now, please.'
steps.prompt: Both end the call. What does the first one do that the second does not?
options: It is more polite because it is longer.
It puts the reason on the speaker's own schedule rather than on the other person's behaviour.
It leaves the other person free to carry on talking.
steps.answer: It puts the reason on the speaker's own schedule rather than on the other person's behaviour.
steps.why: I'd better makes the speaker the one under pressure. Nobody is being told they have talked too long, although they have.

steps.title: Why news starts in the present perfect
steps.html:
A recycled area, seen here in the place it is used most: telling somebody what has happened.

News is normally announced in the present perfect, because the point is that it matters now: Sara has got the job. They have sold the flat.

Once the news is announced, the details move into the past simple, because they are finished events at a known time: She has got the job. She heard on Tuesday and started yesterday.

Just, already and yet belong to this use. Just = a very short time ago; already = sooner than expected; yet = up to now, in questions and negatives, at the end of the sentence.

Been and gone are not the same. He has been to Lisbon — he went and came back. He has gone to Lisbon — he is still there.

steps.title: Example bank.
steps.html:
Ten sentences you could put straight into an email or a call.

You'll never guess what has happened.
Standard opening for news.

Sara has got the job — she found out on Friday.
News, then past simple detail.

I've just come off the phone with the garage.
Just = moments ago.

They've already fixed the engine.
Sooner than expected.

Have you spoken to him yet?
Yet goes at the end.

I haven't heard back yet.
Negative + yet.

We have been to that place by the river — it's excellent.
Been = went and returned.

He has gone to the office, so he won't answer.
Gone = still there.

It has been great talking to you.
Closing a call; the pleasure runs up to now.

I haven't taken up too much of your time, I hope.
Negative present perfect with a phrasal verb.

steps.title: Announcing news, then filling in the detail
steps.html:
1. The facts: your sister got a new job on Tuesday, and she starts in March.
  2. Announce it in the present perfect, because what matters is the situation now: My sister has got a new job.
  3. Add the finished detail in the past simple, because Tuesday is a known past time: She heard on Tuesday.
  4. Anything still ahead goes into a future form: She starts in March.
  5. Result: My sister has got a new job. She heard on Tuesday and she starts in March. Do not write She has heard on Tuesday.

steps.sub: Minority Languages in the British Isles. About seven minutes.

steps.title: Answer the questions about the film.
steps.prompt: Roughly how many people speak Scottish Gaelic?
steps.why: Around 60,000, most of them in the Highlands or on the islands off the north-west coast.

steps.title: Answer the questions about the film.
steps.prompt: Welsh is spoken by roughly what share of the population of Wales?
steps.why: Around 560,000 people, which is almost 20% of the population.

steps.title: Answer the questions about the film.
steps.prompt: What happened to Cornish?
options: It has never had fewer than a thousand speakers.
Its last native speaker died over 240 years ago and it was declared extinct.
It was banned by law in the 19th century.
steps.answer: Its last native speaker died over 240 years ago and it was declared extinct.
steps.why: It survived in place names and has since been revived: three to five hundred people now speak it fluently.

steps.title: Answer the questions about the film.
steps.prompt: What do experts predict for the world's languages?
options: Around 50% of the world's 6,500 languages could be extinct by the end of the century.
The number of languages will roughly double.
English will replace all other languages within fifty years.
steps.answer: Around 50% of the world's 6,500 languages could be extinct by the end of the century.
steps.why: The film gives this as the wider context for the four British cases.

steps.title: What is the film's main argument at the end?
options: Small languages should be recorded and then allowed to die.
You do not have to give up one language in order to speak another.

steps.answer: You do not have to give up one language in order to speak another.

steps.title: Write an informal email giving news.
steps.sub: 140–170 words. You have been away somewhere with almost no phone coverage, and you are catching up with a friend.
steps.html:
• Open by apologising for the delay and giving the reason.
  • Announce your main news in the present perfect.
  • Add the detail in the past simple.
  • Give one more piece of news using <i>just</i>, <i>already</i> or <i>yet</i>.
  • Close with a phrase from the Useful language box.

Useful language

  • Sorry it has taken me so long to get back to you — there was no coverage where we were.
  • You'll never guess what has happened.
  • I've just … / I've already … / I haven't … yet.
  • The big news is that …
  • I've copied Dan in, so he has the details too.
  • I won't take up any more of your time — let's catch up properly soon.
steps.modelHtml:
Hi Maya,

Sorry for the silence — I've just got back from two weeks on La Gomera and there was almost no coverage in the valleys, so nothing sent and nothing arrived.

The big news is that I've finally handed in the thesis. I sent it on the Friday before we left and I still haven't heard anything back, which I am trying not to think about. Ravi has already read the first half and says it is fine, so I am choosing to believe him.

The island itself was extraordinary. I've been to the Canaries twice before but never there. The locals whistle across the ravines — a real language, not a signal — and I confused it with birdsong for the first two days.

I won't take up any more of your Sunday. Let's catch up properly next week.

Nick
